text: Your money lost its gold in 1971, so why hasn't it died? What is it actually backed by?
Look at the small print on a British pound or an Indian rupee and you'll find the same promise.
I promise to pay the bearer.
Pay you what?
In early 1933, a hundred dollar bill was a claim on almost five ounces of gold.
by the 1960s, less than three.
Today, spend it on gold and you'd get about a 40th of an ounce.
Somewhere between those numbers is one Sunday night in 1971,
when that promise quietly changed and never changed back.
So let's follow one banknote through 26 centuries of money
and find out what's really standing behind yours.
Before there was a note, there was a problem.
You have chickens. You want a goat.
The goat owner hates chickens.
Economists call this the double coincidence of wants.
Everyone else calls it a wasted afternoon.
So people tried shells, cattle, metal, and one material kept winning.
Gold. It doesn't rust. It doesn't rot. It's rare, but not too rare. You can melt it, split
it and stamp it, and everyone everywhere already wanted it.
More than 25 centuries ago, in Lydia, in what is now western Turkey, lumps of Electrum,
a natural mix of gold and silver, were stamped with a lion's head. They're among the earliest
coins we know of. No more weighing metal at every sale. You could just count.
But gold had one big problem. It's heavy. Try buying a house with a backpack full of coins.
